summary: We wanted visually impaired people to be able to intuitively explore datasets that reveal the scale and impact that climate change has had on our planet. That's why we developed a cross-platform desktop application that transforms NASA's Earth Information Center 2D visualizations into an informative soundscape that is navigable through an accessible 3D-printed interface, something that they used to only undersatnd through descriptions before.
details:
Climate change is making extreme weather worse and changing the world we live in. Visualizations of climate data help people grasp how big these changes are, and that awareness matters if we're going to work on solutions. NASA's Earth Information Center (EIC) makes striking, insightful visualizations of our planet. But they only work through color and pattern, so at least 43 million blind people worldwide can only learn about them from written descriptions.

TerraGroove makes these visualizations accessible to everyone. It's a cross-platform desktop app that turns NASA EIC 2D visualizations into an interactive soundscape. Users explore it by touching a 3D-printed tactile world map placed on a laptop trackpad. As a finger moves over a region, the app plays music for that exact spot and can give more information about what the data shows there.

The app measures the main color (Red, Orange, Green, Blue, White, Black) tuned to NASA color scales intensity, edge density, shape (uniform, linear, circular, organic) and how spotty/swirly the area is. These features drive a 75 BPM synthesizer in C minor, inspired by Daft Punk's Veridis Quo. Color sets pitch range and instrument. Cool colors play low, soft pads. Warm colors (high CO2, extreme fire risk) move into higher, brighter registers and add a tension note. Density sets rhythm and calm areas hold long notes. Complex areas play fast arpeggios and fuller drum patterns. Shape and swirliness set the melody. Swirling patterns create sweeping melodic turns. Spotty areas trigger off-beat marimba accents and percussion.
